sources.title: Vây Cá Tiếng Anh Là Gì? Hướng Dẫn Toàn Tập Về Các Loại Vây Cá & Chức Năng
Understanding Clamped Fins in Aquarium Fish
Fin Damage - Fish Articles | Furry Critter Network
Tiêu Chuẩn Chọn Lựa Và Cách Nuôi Cá Rồng Kim Long | Pet Mart Cửa Hàng Thú Cưng

facts.fact: Vietnamese name for the term: "Vây lưng".
English name for the term: "Dorsal Fin" (heading: "Dorsal Fin (Vây lưng) – “Bánh lái” phía trên").
English name for the term: "dorsal fin".
The dorsal fin is an unpaired fin on the midline of the back of most fish.
Vây lưng sits on the fish's back and is usually the most visible fin when the fish is seen from above.
The dorsal fin's main job is to help the fish resist rolling and make sudden turns.
Vây lưng works like a ship's rudder: it keeps the fish balanced so it does not roll or spin while swimming, and it helps the fish change direction precisely.
In some species the dorsal fin has sharp, hard spines that the fish uses to defend itself or threaten enemies, and some species raise it to look bigger.
Many catfish use sharp, erect dorsal spines for defence, and in some catfish the spines are venomous.
Depending on the species, a fish has one, two or three dorsal fins. Goldfish have one.
Vây lưng is made of soft rays or hard (spiny) rays, and its shape is an important feature for telling species apart.
In fish the dorsal fin is supported by bones called pterygiophores and carries dermal fin rays called lepidotrichia.
Gymnarchus niloticus swims by moving its long dorsal fin, which runs the whole length of its back, while keeping its back straight for electrolocation.

A Vietnamese pet shop gives the Asian arowana (cá Rồng, Scleropages formosus Kim Long) 15–19 dorsal fin rays ("Vây lưng từ 15 – 19 chiếc") and about 25–27 rays in the rear fin, and uses this in choosing fish.
Clamped fins are fins held tightly against the body instead of spread out. Clamping can affect the dorsal, pectoral, anal and tail fins.
Clamped fins are a sign of stress or illness, not a disease in themselves.

Fins clamp because of poor water quality (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate), wrong temperature, overcrowding, aggressive tankmates, too few hiding places, disease (white spot, velvet, fin rot), poor nutrition, or chemicals such as chlorine, chloramine or medication errors.
For clamped fins, first test the water for ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH and temperature. If anything is off, do a 25–50% water change with dechlorinated water.
After correcting the water, watch the fish for 24–48 hours for other signs such as spots, fraying fins or swelling. Dim the lights, keep disturbance low, and add hiding places.
Clamping from environmental causes often improves within 24–72 hours once conditions are corrected. Only treat with medicine when a specific illness has been identified.
In community aquariums, aggression from tankmates (fin nipping) is the most frequent cause of fin damage. Long-finned fish are frequent targets.
Plastic plants with sharp edges, rough rocks and broken coral can snag and tear fins.
A fin torn mechanically (nipped or snagged) has fairly clean edges, and the tissue around it looks healthy. Fin rot shows discoloured edges and keeps getting worse.
Minor fin damage with clean edges usually heals without treatment within one to two weeks if the water is kept clean.
Most fish can fully regrow damaged fins. This takes from two weeks to several months, and severe or repeated injuries may heal incompletely.

For fin problems, salt is a good first step. Treating bacterial fin infections may need 3 to 5 ppt of salt. If salt fails, the source suggests hydrogen peroxide or peracetic acid products used as their labels direct.
Scaleless fish such as loaches and some catfish should not be given salt treatment for fin damage.
Too few water changes lead to poor water quality and fin rot.
To prevent fin problems, change water regularly, keep conditions stable, avoid overcrowding, choose compatible tankmates, feed a balanced diet, and quarantine new fish for 2–4 weeks.
Do not keep fin-nipping species with long-finned fish, and check all decorations for sharp edges before putting them in the tank.
Giving medicine without a confirmed diagnosis is a mistake: unneeded medication can add stress and make water quality worse.
Assuming the problem is solved while the fins stay clamped is a mistake, because it means the underlying cause is still there.
